about: The one list of Will Cook's websites, films, repositories and how they connect. The home page at wcook04.github.io, its catalogue.json graph and its llms.txt are built from it and from glossary.json. Each website keeps a copy for its own header, footer and film slots. Edit this file, then follow README.md, 'Add a released film'.

owner.name: Will Cook
owner.lede: I do mathematics research and build software with AI agents. I also build ways to inspect what the agents produce.
invitation: I’m looking for a job, internship, fellowship or funding, and I’m open to working with other people on their problems. If there’s a problem you think I should work on, please email me.
If something on these pages is unclear or wrong, please tell me. If your feedback leads to a change, I’d be happy to credit you, with your permission.
owner.orient: That means Lean proofs of AI-written mathematics, websites that display a paper beside its Lean code, and tools for running several coding agents in one repository. The introduction video explains how the projects fit together.
owner.availability: I’m looking for a job, internship, fellowship or research collaboration.

projects_lede: Several projects use Lean, a proof assistant: software that accepts a proof only after verifying every step.

sites.name: Plectis Mathematics
sites.purpose: AI-assisted research on eight Erdős problems, with papers, records of failed approaches and Lean 4 proofs of partial results.
sites.status: Each problem page states whether the original question is still open and which statements the Lean proofs cover.
sites.capture_caption: The front page of Plectis Mathematics, open at problem #68.
sites.credit: Seven original questions remain open. The #1041 formal-statement counterexample is due to ani. The papers are not peer reviewed.
sites.label: Maths Map
sites.subject: eight Erdős problems
sites.tagline: Maths Map: AI-assisted research on eight Erdős problems, with Lean proofs
sites.summary: Browse theorems from eight Erdős problems on one map, open each in a long research record or a short paper, and see which statements Lean or Comparator accepted and which original questions stay open.
sites.line: Eight Erdős problems on one map: each theorem, its paper and its Lean check.

sites.name: SK Reader
sites.purpose: Three explanations of OpenAI’s full-support theorem for the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass, linked to Lean declarations and an argument map.
sites.status: The site lists each Lean build and the statements it covers. Comparator gave no verdict on either theorem.
sites.capture_caption: The short paper at Theorem 1, beside the graph of its argument.
sites.credit: The theorem and Lean proof are OpenAI’s. I made the explanations and links with AI; no mathematician has reviewed them.
sites.label: SK Reader
sites.subject: spin glasses
sites.tagline: SK Reader: OpenAI's spin-glass Lean proof beside three readable papers
sites.summary: Read three AI-written papers on OpenAI's Sherrington–Kirkpatrick theorem, click a ticked statement to open OpenAI's Lean, and follow a 131-step argument map. AI agents wrote the map and 799 links; no mathematician has reviewed them.
sites.line: In large Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glasses, two near-best states can differ in half their spins.

sites.name: General Reader
sites.purpose: Read Contextual Embeddings (PLDI 2026) beside its authors’ Lean proof, with statement-to-code links and a graph of proof dependencies.
sites.capture_caption: Contextual Embeddings on the left page, with the graph of its Lean proof and the exact lines on the right.
sites.credit: Paper and proof by Frohlich, Foster, Kavvos and Wang. I made the reader and links with AI; the authors have not reviewed the links.
sites.label: General Reader
sites.subject: any paper beside its Lean
sites.tagline: General Reader: a published paper beside its authors' Lean proof
sites.summary: Click a sentence in Contextual Embeddings (PLDI 2026) to open the authors' Lean lines it describes, with a graph and axiom list from Lean's own report. Will added the links with AI; it works for any paper with public Lean.
sites.line: Click a sentence in a paper to open the lines of Lean proof it describes.

sites.name: Quartic Reader
sites.purpose: Lean 4 formalisation of OpenAI’s nearly quartic randomized–quantum query-complexity separation, with mathematical expositions and a paragraph-linked proof reader.
sites.status: Comparator accepted each proof bundle in local runs on my computer and rejected five deliberately wrong solutions. The Forrelation lower bound, which the preprint imports, is proved here by a shorter route in a weaker form.
sites.capture_caption: The general reader beside the graph of the Lean proof, following the paragraph being read.
sites.credit: Original theorem by OpenAI; formalisation and explanations made with AI. No human has reviewed whether the Lean statements match the paper.
sites.label: Quartic Reader
sites.subject: quantum queries
sites.tagline: Quartic Reader: OpenAI's randomized-versus-quantum query separation, proved in Lean 4
sites.summary: About 29,000 lines of AI-written Lean 4 prove OpenAI's nearly quartic separation; Comparator accepted the main theorem and rejected five broken proofs. Each paper passage lists its Lean statements, labelled by AI as exact, stronger or partial matches.
sites.line: OpenAI’s nearly quartic gap between randomized and quantum query complexity, proved in Lean 4.

sites.name: Plectis Atlas

routes.label: Example: two reports on a paper about π

sites.purpose: An index of OpenAI’s mathematics manuscripts, Lean statement files and published assessments, grouped into 372 paper families.
sites.status: I drafted the matches between each Lean statement and its paper with AI; no person has reviewed them.
sites.capture_caption: The Atlas map: each circle is a subject and each dot a family of papers.
sites.credit: Reports credited to MathVet, Carlos Toledo’s cert-machine and Neal McBurnett. I assembled the index and statement links with AI.
sites.label: Atlas
sites.subject: OpenAI’s maths papers, reviewed
sites.tagline: Plectis Atlas: OpenAI's maths papers beside outside groups' assessments
sites.summary: Browse or search OpenAI's 719 current maths papers, grouped into 372 families on a subject map, and read each outside group's coverage label and report, credited to that group. Atlas has not rerun the groups' proof checks.
sites.line: OpenAI’s 719 maths papers, and how outside groups assessed each paper’s Lean statement.

sites.name: Practical Formal Verification

routes.label: Which proofs and tests cover each one

sites.purpose: Dafny proofs for 16 selected computations in an 88-component research-workflow prototype, with generated Python and proof-coverage maps.
sites.capture_caption: The system map: the 88 components in their seven families.
sites.credit: The proofs cover those computations, not the complete system.
sites.label: Formal verification
sites.subject: Dafny proofs of a toolkit
sites.tagline: Practical Formal Verification: Dafny proofs inside an 88-component research toolkit
sites.summary: Dafny proofs cover 16 selected computations, 12 inside particular components and four shared, compiled to Python. A map shows each kind of evidence for each component separately; whole-claim coverage reads unknown for all 88.
sites.line: 88 Python components of a toolkit; Dafny proofs for 16 of their calculations.

sites.name: Zenith
sites.purpose: Experiments on whether records of earlier mistakes help language models test and repair code. A held-out study found 77.0% versus 69.2% fault-class detection.
sites.status: The held-out study used DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The earlier website and PDF describe separate studies, including program repairs rising from 259 to 365 of 576 tasks.
sites.capture_caption: The opening of the Zenith paper.
sites.credit: One model on 58 HumanEval problems; about half the gain came from timeouts. Study available in an unmerged branch.
sites.label: Zenith
sites.subject: AI testers and missed bugs
sites.tagline: Zenith measures whether showing an AI model its missed bugs improves testing
sites.summary: A pre-registered study in which DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, given records of EvalPlus bugs it missed on 28 practice problems, caught 77% rather than 69% on 58 held-out problems; about half the rise came from timeouts. Every prompt and reply is published.
sites.line: Shown the bugs it missed, a model’s score on 58 new problems rose from 69% to 77%.

sites.name: Code Ontology Bridge
sites.purpose: Exports Python code structure to DuckDB, with semantic descriptions and recursive SQL views for NVIDIA Auto Ontology’s text-to-SQL agent.
sites.status: AI models wrote the questions and answer keys; 21 answer keys were corrected after the runs. Every question, answer and failed run is published.
sites.capture_caption: Calls followed backwards from a function, with a callback reference shown dashed.
sites.credit: Independent of NVIDIA. Descriptions helped DeepSeek in a 48-question direct-prompt study; no clear improvement in the 12-question Auto Ontology study.
sites.label: Code Ontology Bridge
sites.subject: for NVIDIA Auto Ontology
sites.tagline: Code Ontology Bridge exports call graphs to DuckDB for NVIDIA Auto Ontology
sites.summary: Runs static analysis on Python source, writes functions and calls to DuckDB with semantic models for NVIDIA Auto Ontology's text-to-SQL agent, and publishes a 48-question study where every answer is a rerunnable SQL query. Independent of NVIDIA.
sites.line: With this DuckDB code database, NVIDIA Auto Ontology answered 10.3 of 12 questions; DeepSeek alone, 3.2.

projects.name: Agent Trace
projects.purpose: Local Codex and Claude Code session viewer with tool traces, selective context export and optional MCP access.
projects.credit: Technical preview; browser app or native Mac window.
projects.label: Agent Trace
projects.subject: Claude Code and Codex sessions
projects.tagline: Agent Trace opens saved Codex and Claude Code sessions with their commands
projects.summary: Lists local Codex and Claude Code conversation files, shows each command beside its saved status, exit code and output, and copies chosen conversations at a chosen level of detail; an optional MCP server gives agents the same records. Copied text is not redacted.
projects.line: Every Claude Code and Codex session on your computer, each command beside its output.

projects.name: Narration IR
projects.purpose: A skill for building an intermediate representation (IR) between a transcript and a visual specification. The IR adds source-grounded metadata about what the words mean, what viewers need to understand and when visual events should happen, giving an animation agent context for generating visuals.
projects.label: Narration IR
projects.subject: narration into picture plans
projects.tagline: A portable agent skill for word-timed plans of narrated explanations
projects.summary: Before an AI writes animation code, it writes a plan stating what each spoken sentence means and which recorded word times each picture change. A bundled program confirms each quote is in its source file; a person reads the meanings.
projects.line: Each spoken sentence gets its meaning, word-timed picture events and quotes from its sources.

projects.name: Safety Core
projects.purpose: Generates AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and command-enforcement hooks from one rulebook, distinguishing written instructions from rules enforced by hooks.
projects.credit: Tested in one small Claude Haiku study; the enforcement rule was written after observing the failure.
projects.label: Safety Core
projects.subject: a rulebook for coding agents
projects.tagline: Safety Core turns one rulebook into coding-agent instructions and command hooks
projects.summary: Builds AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and Claude Code hooks from one editable rulebook adapting ideas from Anthropic's Claude Constitution, and maps rules to files. In one small Claude Haiku 4.5 test, 10 of 10 runs committed without it and 0 of 10 with hooks.
projects.line: A written rule cut an agent’s bad commits from 10 runs in 10 to 6; a command check, to 0.

projects.name: One Checkout
projects.purpose: Commits a reviewed Git patch while preserving another agent’s unfinished staged and working-tree edits, including changes in the same files.
projects.label: One Checkout
projects.subject: commit one fix among many edits
projects.tagline: One Checkout commits one reviewed git patch while other agents keep editing
projects.summary: Applies a coding agent's git patch to the last commit so the agent can test that version, then commits it while another agent's unfinished staged and working-tree edits stay. It skips git hooks and does not prevent overwrites.
projects.line: Commit one agent’s finished patch while another agent’s unfinished edits stay in the same file.

projects.name: CodeMap
projects.purpose: A code browser with docstring descriptions and function-call links, available to both the human reader and coding agents.
projects.status: Not released; the video shows it in use.
projects.credit: Private software; the video shows it in use.
projects.label: CodeMap
projects.subject: a map of AI-written code
projects.tagline: Code Map shows code files with their saved descriptions and call links
projects.summary: A private interface where each file is a box containing the docstring description coding agents write and update under fixed headings, with links to code that calls each function; agents fetch the same descriptions as text. Descriptions can be wrong or out of date.
projects.line: A map of a codebase, drawn from the descriptions coding agents save in each file.

projects.name: The funnel
projects.label: The funnel
projects.subject: AI-written maths into papers and films
projects.purpose: How AI-written mathematics becomes a long research record, a specialist paper, a plain explanation, a video and a reader website.
projects.tagline: Instructions AI follows to rewrite Lean-checked maths for each kind of reader
projects.summary: AI, following written instructions, turns a proof Lean has accepted into a long research record, a specialist paper, an exposition and a video. Worked examples are Erdős problem #257 and OpenAI's results on the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass and the nearly quartic quantum query separation.
projects.line: One Lean-checked proof of Erdős #257 becomes a 152-page record, two papers and a video.

films.title: Introduction (V3): I still want to understand what AI builds
films.description: I use AI for maths research and software, and build interfaces so other people can follow the results.
films.takeaway: Goes through the maths funnel, the Atlas, Lean Exposition and Maths Map websites, CodeMap, One Checkout, Plectis's 88 Python components, Safety Core and Zenith, all prototypes.

films.title: Introduction (V1, older version): How the projects fit together
films.description: An older introduction. Watch the latest Introduction (V3) from the home page. I go through the maths, the code map, how I make these videos, and the tools I use to manage the agents. Then some research into how the agents could improve their own way of working.
films.takeaway: Goes through CodeMap's architecture, focus and blast views, One Checkout, the funnel on eight Erdős problems, Atlas, the Demo Take video editor, Safety Core and Zenith, all prototypes.

films.title: Maths Map: eight Erdős problems on one map
films.description: I use one problem, Erdős #257, to show where its proof, papers and explanation video are on the Maths Map.
films.takeaway: Follows Erdős problem #257 on Maths Map from Comparator-checked theorems down through its long research record, short specialist paper and expository paper to its explanation video.

films.title: Erdős #257: why some infinite sums cannot be fractions
films.description: I explain a known irrationality result for Erdős #257, starting with 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15, and so on.
films.takeaway: Proves from fractions upwards that every infinite choice from 1, 1/3, 1/7, 1/15, ... whose exponents' reciprocals add to a finite total sums to an irrational number.

films.title: Lean Exposition: read a maths paper beside its argument map
films.description: I show how to read a maths explanation beside a map of its assumptions, results and sources.
films.takeaway: Shows the SK Reader website, where scrolling an AI-written paper on the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick result highlights the matching step on an argument map, and linked passages open across papers.

films.title: Spin glasses: how different can two nearly best answers be?
films.description: I explain how two nearly best arrangements of magnets can differ, starting with four arrows.
films.takeaway: Scores all 16 arrangements of a four-arrow magnet board by hand, then states when two nearly best Sherrington–Kirkpatrick arrangements differing in half their arrows almost surely exist.

films.title: Atlas: why two people gave one OpenAI maths paper different verdicts on its completeness
films.description: In two reports on an OpenAI paper about π, both groups say Comparator accepted the Lean proof, but they label the Lean statement’s coverage differently. I go through what each label means.
films.takeaway: Reads two groups' reports on OpenAI's paper showing π has irrationality exponent 2, and traces their full and narrower coverage labels to an omitted Flint Hills series claim.

films.title: Formal verification: what does this check actually prove?
films.description: On a map of the 88 Python components, I show what each Dafny proof and saved result covers.
films.takeaway: Goes through every evidence ring on the 88-component map, opens one Dafny-proved calculation to read what its proof leaves out, and follows one design rule to components.

films.title: Zenith: I showed an AI tester the bugs it missed
films.description: I test whether an AI code tester catches more bugs after seeing a record of its earlier misses.
films.takeaway: With records of the EvalPlus bugs it missed, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash caught 77% of bugs rather than 69% on 58 new problems; rules it wrote did not help.

films.title: Safety Core: my AI agent made up a setting to pass a test
films.description: I give a coding agent written rules and command-blocking hooks, then record what it does to get past a failing test.
films.takeaway: Shows Safety Core's rulebook and map, and Claude Haiku 4.5 committing with a made-up setting in 10 of 10 runs, 6 under written rules, none under hooks.

films.title: One Checkout: when Claude is done and Codex is still editing
films.description: I show how to commit one fix while another agent's unfinished edits stay in the same file.
films.takeaway: Follows Claude's login fix into a commit while Codex's edits stay, and shows a commit from Codex's older staged copy putting the old login code back.

films.title: CodeMap: finding my way through code written with AI
films.description: I follow a code search from a file's saved description to the function and the code that calls it.
films.takeaway: Follows one search in Code Map from the Find box to the function that finds matching files and the code calling it, via saved docstrings and call links.

films.title: Introduction (V2, older version): Using AI for maths research and software
films.description: An older introduction. Watch the latest Introduction (V3) from the home page. In this video I introduce the projects and explain how they fit together, from computer-checked proofs and papers to maps and videos you can follow yourself.
films.takeaway: An earlier introduction to the projects and how they fit together, from computer-checked proofs and papers to maps and videos a viewer can follow.

films.title: How much faster can a quantum computer be? OpenAI's fourth-power result
films.description: I compare how many times quantum and classical computers must look at the same data, then explain why four is the best possible power for total yes-or-no questions.
films.takeaway: Shows one photon comparing two hidden bits in one quantum query, then explains OpenAI's hidden-certificate and weighted-pivot construction proving the fourth power optimal, and compares each Lean statement.
